web_evidence.title: Of Mice and Men — Distributed Proofreaders Canada eBook
web_evidence.note: The complete legally posted Canadian public-domain text consistently uses an external narrator across the opening, interior, and ending; first-person forms are confined to character speech.

web_evidence.title: The Great Depression in John Steinbeck’s Of Mice and Men
web_evidence.note: This university thesis analyzes the novella's six-chapter structure and explicitly identifies its narrator as third-person omniscient and nonjudgmental.

web_evidence.title: Enablers of and barriers to reading in Key Stage 3 English: a participatory case study using Reader Response to explore reader interaction with fiction
web_evidence.note: The doctoral thesis closely analyzes the first five paragraphs and identifies third-person address and an onlooker-like, filmic narrational style; its scope is limited to the opening.

web_evidence.title: Of Mice and Men
web_evidence.note: The critical overview describes the novel's point of view as generally objective, not aligned with one character, and explicitly third-person.

web_evidence.title: Of Mice and Men: Point of View
web_evidence.note: The dedicated point-of-view analysis explicitly classifies the novella as omniscient third-person and notes its objective descriptions of spaces without characters present.

person_note: The Goodreads evidence contains many first-person, plural, and generic second-person forms, but all occur in character dialogue and therefore do not identify the base narrator. Quotes q00021 and q00026 independently show sustained external scene narration, while shorter event descriptions remain conservatively unmarked. The complete web text and academic structural analysis agree that the controlling narrator is nonparticipating and third-person, with no first-person frame or sustained alternate-person section. Sources differ only over the subtype—objective versus omniscient—which does not affect the THIRD classification.
